session-decisions now reads a per-clone forge override from git config ([#70](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/70), for [#60](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/60)):

```
git config tracker.forge forgejo
git config tracker.web https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo
```

The keys are named `tracker.*` so that forge-tracker can read them too. forge-tracker still works out the forge only from `origin` and its own `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` (`forge:`). A repo whose remote is an SSH alias, a mirror or a push-only URL therefore gets correct links from session-decisions and still fails or misreads in `/catchup` and `/next`.

forge-tracker should read `tracker.forge` and `tracker.web` with `git config --get`, with the same precedence session-decisions uses:
- `tracker.web` replaces the remote's host and path;
- `tracker.forge` sets the kind;
- both win over the built-in host rules.

Its existing `forge:` key in `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` should either defer to `tracker.forge` or be documented as the committed per-repo default, with git config as the per-clone override. The API base for a self-hosted forge (and any pinned CA) still comes from forge-tracker's own config, since git config holds only the web base.
response.title: forge-tracker: read the per-clone tracker.forge and tracker.web git config keys

response.body:
A clone can now say which forge its `#12` and `!4` references link to, ahead of `forge_hosts` and the built-in host rules:

```bash
git config tracker.forge forgejo
git config tracker.web https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo
```

## Why git config

I weighed the three places [#60](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/60) names:

- **git config** is per clone, which is where an SSH host alias belongs (it comes from one machine's `~/.ssh/config`, so a committed file would be wrong for other clones). git parses it, the plugin reads it with one more `git` call next to the remote lookup, and forge-tracker's Python can read it with `git config --get` and no parser. `includeIf "hasconfig:remote.*.url:..."` in `~/.gitconfig` can apply `tracker.forge` to every clone of an alias.
- **Project-scoped plugin options** are per plugin, so forge-tracker couldn't read session-decisions' value without reaching into another plugin's settings, and `.claude/settings.json` is committed.
- **A `.claude/` file**: forge-tracker already has `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` with a `forge:` key, but its loader rejects unknown keys (there's no `web:`), session-decisions would need a frontmatter parser, and a committed file has the same alias problem.

The keys are `tracker.*`, not `session-decisions.*`, so both plugins can read them. Magit Forge already uses the `forge.*` section, so I avoided that one.

## Behaviour

- `tracker.web` set: it is the repository (`https://` only), and the remote isn't read. The kind is `tracker.forge`, or else whatever `forge_hosts` and the built-in rules say of the web host.
- Only `tracker.forge` set: the remote's host and path on that kind of forge.
- Neither set: the existing behaviour, unchanged.
- A subpath works for GitHub and Forgejo (`https://code.example.org/forge/me/tool`, cross-repo refs included). For GitLab the whole path is the project, so `group/project#7` misses a subpath; the README says so.
- A value it can't use gets a toast at session start, the same way `forge_hosts` does, and is ignored.

The pure logic (`parseOverride`, `webForge`, `resolveForge`) lives in `hooks/forge.ts` with tests; `register.tsx` reads `git config --get-regexp '^tracker\.(forge|web)$'` at session start.

## Verified

- `claude plugin test plugins/session-decisions`: 93 pass. `claude plugin validate --strict plugins/session-decisions` passes.
- On screen with term-recorder: Claude Code 2.1.300, Sonnet, `--plugin-dir` on this branch, in a scratch repo whose `origin` is `homelab-git:lokkju/demo.git` with both keys set. One `DECIDE ... [#12]` task drew the D1 card, and the cast has the OSC 8 hyperlink `https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo/issues/12` on its `#12`.
- The `includeIf hasconfig` glob in the README (`homelab-git:*/**`) was checked against git 2.43; `homelab-git:**` doesn't match a path with a slash.

forge-tracker doesn't read the keys yet; that's a follow-up there.

Closes #60

response.body:
Part of #12 (forge-tracker). A read-only forge layer that the briefing and grooming commands use. It is filed as its own piece, because the three commands built on it each need the same reads on all three forges.

**The forges.** GitHub (`gh`, REST plus GraphQL where REST is thin), GitLab (`glab api`, including self-hosted with a subpath and a pinned CA) and Forgejo/Gitea (`tea` where it covers the read, otherwise the REST API with the user's token). Each forge is detected from the repo's remote, the same way #12 already plans.

**What every adapter answers, in one normalized shape:**
- **Identity:** the authenticated user, and whether an account is a bot.
- **Issues:** open issues, and issues updated since a time. Each carries labels, milestone (title, due date), assignees, created/updated/closed timestamps and comments since a time.
- **Links between issues:** native blocking where the forge has it (GitHub "blocked by" issue dependencies and sub-issues, Forgejo dependencies, GitLab `blocks` on tiers that have it). Where it doesn't (GitLab CE has only `relates_to`), a configurable convention such as `relates_to` plus a `blocked` label.
- **PRs/MRs:** open, and merged since a time. Each carries title, source branch, merge commit sha, reviewers/assignees, draft and conflict state, and head pipeline status.
- **CI:** the newest pipeline/workflow run on the default branch by trigger (push vs schedule), its failed jobs, and jobs that passed only on retry.
- **Branches:** remote branch heads, and which have no open PR/MR.
- **Tags/releases:** the newest tags and releases. Container registry tags are optional, and only where configured.

**Rules learned building this once:**
- **GET only, enforced at the boundary.** The adapter's transport refuses any method but GET, so a read-only command can't write even by mistake.
- **Paginate to the end, or fail loudly.** A page cap that is hit is a FAILED read, never a silently short list that renders as "none".
- **Every read can fail on its own.** It returns data or a named error, and callers print `<part>: FAILED (<reason>)`, never an empty section.
- **The shared account.** Agents usually authenticate as the user, so nothing may treat "the user's account did X" as "the user did X", and no assignee is a signal that a human must act.
- **No secrets in errors.** Error text includes the CLI's stderr truncated, never tokens.
- **Injectable fetch.** Tests feed canned payloads per forge, with no network.

**Done when:** each forge's adapter passes the same contract test suite over recorded fixtures, plus one live read-only smoke run per forge.
response.title: forge-tracker: a read-only forge layer for GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo

response.body:
Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21). Like `/catchup`, it can ship for one forge first.

**`/next`** recommends what to work on: the user's own queue, work agents can start now, and what is blocked. It is read-only. It recommends, and never claims, assigns, comments or branches.

**Two layers, both cached outside the repo** under `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/<plugin>/next/<host>_<project>/`:
1. **Facts (a script).**
   - **What it reads:** open issues with tier, due date, labels, owners and links; open PRs/MRs with head pipeline and conflict state; branches with no PR/MR.
   - **How it caches:** under a fingerprint of cheap inputs. These are the default-branch head, the newest issue, PR and pipeline `updated_at`, open issue and PR counts, a digest of the milestones (id, title, due date), the remote branch heads, and a schema tag that hashes the code itself. When the fingerprint is unchanged, the cached facts are reused, so a rerun takes seconds. A run with a failed read is written but never reused.
2. **The slate (Claude's ranking).** It is stored with the facts' fingerprint and shown again unchanged until the fingerprint moves.
   - **The user's queue:** person-only items, ordered by how many agent-ready items each one unblocks, counted transitively through blocking links and cycle-safe.
   - **Agent lanes:** unblocked agent-ready items by tier and due date, grouped into lanes that shouldn't touch the same files. The grouping is a stated judgement, not a measurement. A lane that already has an open PR or a pushed branch is marked in flight.
   - **Blocked:** each blocked item and what it waits on.

**Classification rules learned the hard way:**
- **What person-only means:** the configured decision or needs-human labels, plus configurable keyword markers (e.g. hardware, legal).
- **Not person-only:** an assignee is never a reason, because agents share the user's account. Show the assignee as an owner. Some markers are only hints Claude may overrule; design work an agent can build is one example.
- **Merged-but-open issues inflate the ready list badly.** Flag issues that a merged PR/MR references but that are still open. That check, and fixing it, belongs to `/groom` (#22).

**Future enhancement, not now:** a status pane that shows the slate's top items, its age and a "stale" flag when the fingerprint moves. It reads only the cache, and shares a display mechanism with the session-decisions pane.

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21). Each command can ship for one forge first, but the layer is what makes it work on GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo alike.

**`/catchup`** is for coming back to a project after time away: what changed, and what is waiting on you. It is read-only: no claims, comments or merges.

**The window:**
- It starts where the user's previous successful `/catchup` ended, kept in a local marker. **Not** at "your last forge activity": agents act under the user's account, and in practice that gives a four-minute window opening at an agent's last push.
- The marker lives under `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/<plugin>/catchup/<host>_<project>_<user>.json`. The directory is 0700 and files 0600, writes are atomic, and a relative XDG value is ignored.
- The next window starts a few minutes before the marker, so a fast local clock can't skip events. Seeing an event twice is harmless.
- The marker moves only when every read succeeded, and only after the report has printed. A failed print restores the old marker.
- With no marker, the first run covers 7 days. `--since` is an ad-hoc look back that neither reads nor moves the marker. `--no-mark` gives a dry look, and agents must use it whenever they run the command for their own purposes.

**Sections, in order:**
1. **Waiting on you.**
   - Mentions of you in the window, and open PRs/MRs where you are reviewer or assignee.
   - Issues assigned to you and issues carrying the configured needs-a-human and decision labels. Only items created or updated in the window are listed in full; the standing backlog is one count line per list.
   - An issue on several lists is listed once and counted in each. `--all` lists everything.
2. **Merged since:** PRs/MRs merged in the window, grouped by the issue numbers in their titles or branches (ignore date-shaped branch segments). It also covers changelog entries added, where the repo has a configured changelog or records file.
3. **Decisions made:** comments in the window matching a configured ruling pattern, e.g. `Ruling (YYYY-MM-DD):`.
4. **Board movement:** issues opened and closed, counted by the configured priority tiers (labels first, milestone as fallback).
5. **Health:** the default branch's newest push pipeline/run and its failed jobs, a failed scheduled run on its own line, flaky jobs (passed only on retry more than once), and the configured release/registry tags.

**Output:** text by default, `--json` for the same data. Exit 0 only when every read succeeded. The slash command tells Claude to summarize with Waiting on you first, to state every FAILED part plainly, and to act on nothing unless asked.

**Config** (in forge-tracker's per-repo file): tier labels or milestone prefixes, the needs-human, decision and blocked label names, the ruling pattern, the changelog path, and the tags to report.

A session-decisions test run on Claude Code 2.1.300 (`--model haiku`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`) queued its hand-offs with `decision_add` instead of TaskCreate. I took that for missing task tools at first; they weren't missing.

**What changed in 2.1.300.** The `haiku` alias now resolves to `claude-haiku-5-5` (2.1.286 had `haiku:{default:"claude-haiku-4-5"}`; 2.1.300 has `haiku:{default:"claude-haiku-5-5",per_provider:{bedrock:"claude-haiku-4-5",vertex:"claude-haiku-4-5",...}}`). The gate itself is unchanged; it's the same function under new minified names:

```js
function TV(){if(hc()||YUo())return!0;let e=$Lt();if(e===void 0||p6r(e)||f6r(e))return!0;return a.CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS===!0}
function roe(){return NP()&&TV()}   // NP(): false only when CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TASKS is false
```

The model allow-list (`c6r`) still stops at `claude-haiku-4-5`, so haiku now needs the env var like every other Claude 5 model. TaskCreate, TaskUpdate, TaskList and TaskGet are `shouldDefer:!0` in both 2.1.286 and 2.1.300, so with the env var they arrive in the deferred-tool list, not the initial one.

**What I checked** (one short turn each, 100x30 via term-record, plus two `-p` runs):

| Model (`--model`) | Mode | `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS` | Task tools |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| haiku (Haiku 5.5) | interactive | unset | absent |
| haiku (Haiku 5.5) | interactive | 1 | all four, deferred |
| sonnet (Sonnet 5.5) | interactive | unset | absent |
| sonnet (Sonnet 5.5) | interactive | 1 | all four, deferred |
| haiku (Haiku 5.5) | `-p` | unset | absent (init lists only `Task`, `TaskStop`) |
| haiku (Haiku 5.5) | `-p` | 1 | all four, deferred |

The failing run's transcript has `deferred_tools_delta` naming TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList and TaskUpdate, so the session had them. The model called `ToolSearch` with `select:mcp__session-decisions__decision_add` straight after the hand-off nudge, which said "goes in the decision queue with TaskCreate (or decision_add)".

**Changes.**

- `hooks/handoff.ts`: the nudge says TaskCreate is a deferred tool to load with ToolSearch, and that decision_add is only for a session without TaskCreate. With this change, the same two-turn scenario on Haiku 5.5 called `ToolSearch select:TaskCreate` and then TaskCreate for A1 and A2 (one run, so this is evidence, not proof).
- session-decisions README: notes that `haiku` is Haiku 5.5 on the Anthropic API since 2.1.300.
- term-recorder SKILL.md: the task-tool note covers `-p` too, says haiku is a Claude 5 model now, and says the tools are deferred.

`record-demo.sh` already sets `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1` and defaults to sonnet, so it needed no change.

When a repo has no `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md`, the plugin degrades quietly and never offers to fix it. It just emits parenthetical notes, every run, forever.

First use on `eltorocorp/terraform-et-github` at `2026.10.15.3`, with no config file present:

```
/catchup
  (labels.needs_human isn't set, so needs-human issues aren't listed)
  (labels.decision isn't set, so decision issues aren't listed)
  (ruling_pattern isn't set, so rulings aren't picked out)

/next
  Your queue
    nothing person-only
  (labels.needs_human isn't set, so no label marks needs-human items)
  (labels.decision isn't set, so no label marks decision items)
```

The notes are honest, and I would not want them removed. The problem is that nothing ever converts them into configuration.

## Why it matters more than a missing nicety

`Your queue: nothing person-only` is the headline of `/next`, and with no labels configured it is **structurally incapable of being anything else**. The queue is populated from `labels.needs_human`, `labels.decision` and person-only markers; with none set, the only path left is a marker word in a body. So the report's most prominent line reads as "nothing needs you" when what it means is "no label was configured to say so."

Someone reading it quickly — which is the whole point of a catchup — takes the wrong conclusion. The degradation is silent in effect even though it is documented in a footnote.

## Ask

On the first activation or first use in a session, when no `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` exists for the repo, ask whether the user wants to configure it, and offer to write it.

The machinery is mostly there already. `config.py` knows the full key set — `LABEL_KEYS = ("needs_human", "decision", "decision_made", "blocked", "agent")` plus `ruling_pattern` and friends — and the commands already detect and report which are unset. What is missing is the prompt and the writer.

A good version would be concrete rather than open-ended, since the useful answer depends on labels that already exist on the forge: read the repo's actual label list, propose plausible mappings from it (`needs-human`, `needs-decision`, `blocked`, `agent` or whatever is really there), and let the user confirm, correct or skip. Offering a free-text config file to fill in by hand is the version people decline.

## Constraints worth keeping

Ask **once** per repo and remember a decline, so the prompt does not reappear every session; a nag is worse than the footnotes. `/catchup` and `/next` are documented read-only, so the prompt belongs at activation or behind an explicit confirmation, and writing the file should be the only side effect. A repo that genuinely has no such labels should be able to record that fact, so the footnotes stop rather than persisting as noise.

response.body:
On a repo with no `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md`, the reports printed two or three parenthetical notes every run and nothing turned them into configuration. `/next`'s `Your queue: nothing person-only` read as "nothing needs you" when it meant no label was configured to say so.

What changes:

- **One `setup:` line.** Both reports replace their per-key notes with a single line that names what's missing, what the report can't do without it, and how to set it up (`forge-tracker labels suggest`). `/next` appends `(but labels aren't configured to mark any; see setup)` to an empty queue. The Decisions made section of `/catchup` points at the setup line.
- **`~` records "none".** A label key or `ruling_pattern` set to `~` (or `null`) records that the repo has no such label or convention, and the reports drop the line. A quoted `'null'` is still a label name.
- **`forge-tracker labels suggest`** reads the repo's labels (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/labels`, through the read transport) and prints a proposed file: roles matched by name patterns (`needs-human`, `human`, `needs-decision`, `decision`, `question`, `decided`, `blocked`, `on-hold`, `agent-ready`, `agent`, ...), the largest priority family as tiers (`P0`.., `priority:N`, `priority: high`), `~` for each unmatched role, and a `gh label create` command for each. An existing file keeps its values, and the proposal lists only the keys it lacks. It writes nothing; `--json` prints the same data.
- **`forge-tracker labels decline`** records a no in `${XDG_CACHE_HOME}/forge-tracker/setup/<host>_<project>.json` (0600, no forge read, no token). The setup line then says `Setup was declined on <date>`.
- **`/catchup` and `/next`** offer setup once when the line is present and not declined (and not for an agent's own run). They show the proposal, write `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` only on the user's yes, and on a no run `labels decline`. There's no write layer yet, so missing labels on the forge stay `gh label create` commands for the user to run. The reports themselves remain read-only.

The two report modules change only where they built the old notes: two short swaps in `catchup.py`, plus the note swap and the empty-queue suffix in `next.py`. `forges/github.py` gains a `labels()` read and `model.py` a `Label`. The recorded `/next` golden changes in its queue and note lines only.

Tests: matching, tier families, quoting round-trips through the parser, the proposed file loading and silencing the setup line, merge with an existing file, the CLI over a fake label list (GET only, nothing written), a failed read, and decline (0600 file, no `gh` call). README and spec updated.

Closes #59

response.body:
The skill says that every question or step only the user can do goes in the queue in the same turn. Nothing enforces it. An assistant can end a reply with a "left for you" list (merge these PRs, run this on each host) and queue none of it. Wording alone relies on the model applying the rule at the moment it writes the closing list, and that is where it slips. The usual rationalization is that a step the assistant could do on request (merging a PR) isn't "only the user's".

## Proposal

- **A `classic.Stop` handler in `hooks/register.tsx`.** It reads `last_assistant_message` and skips when `stop_hook_active` is set. It finds hand-off lines that carry no `D<n>`/`A<n>` label: phrases such as "left for you", "you'll need to", "your call" and "next steps", plus the bullets or numbered items that follow them. When it finds any, it returns `block` with a reason that quotes those lines and says to queue them and rewrite the reply. The reason also says to ignore a match that isn't a hand-off.
- **The detector in `hooks/queue.ts` or `hooks/subject.ts`,** as plain data, with tests for:
  - hand-offs with labels
  - hand-offs without labels
  - prose that only resembles one
- **One line in SKILL.md:** anything handed back to the user counts, including merges and per-host steps the assistant could do if asked.
- **Release:** a minor version, 2.1.0.

## Costs and open questions

- It adds one model pass to each reply where it fires.
- Phrase matching misfires both ways. The phrase list and the threshold need tuning against real transcripts before it blocks by default. One option is to start it as an `additionalContext` nudge rather than a block.
- It's unclear whether the fallback-ledger mode (no TaskCreate) needs the same check, since its replies already end with a list of open items.

Found while settling the last question on [lokkju/skills#13](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/13), on Claude Code 2.1.286 in headless `claude -p` runs with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1` and `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`, session-decisions 2026.10.15.1 installed.

**What happens.** The parent creates D1 with TaskCreate. A background subagent (`Agent` with `run_in_background: true`) is told the user answered D1 and to settle it. The subagent has no TaskUpdate: it isn't in its tool list and `ToolSearch` `select:TaskUpdate` answers "No matching deferred tools found". So it calls `decision_close`, which refuses:

> session-decisions: D1 is a task-list item; mark it completed with TaskUpdate and add the ruling to its description. If TaskUpdate is deferred, load it with ToolSearch first.

The ruling is recorded nowhere and the task file stays pending. `decision_update` goes through the same `TaskUpdate` check, so I'd expect it to dead-end the same way (not run).

**Why.** `taskUpdateOffered()` in `hooks/register.tsx` asks `$.tool.list()`. A probe hook logged that list inside the subagent's `decision_close` call (the `tool.call` event carried the subagent's `agentId`), and it named TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskStop and TaskUpdate: the main loop's tools, not the subagent's. The declaration says "the tools the model can call now", which isn't what it returned for a subagent's loop.

**Related, documentation only.** A background subagent gets no TaskCreate either, so its items go through `decision_add` and are ledger items: they share the parent's queue and counter (the subagent's item came back as D2 after the parent's D1) but never appear in ctrl+t, even though the parent's do. The README's "Without them" paragraph and the ctrl+t limit describe a session with no task tools; they don't cover a session whose background subagents lack them. A foreground subagent does get TaskCreate, and its items land in the parent's task list with the parent's labels.

The fix is the maintainer's call; options I can see are deciding from the loop (`e.agentId` is set on a subagent's `tool.call`, and `$.agent.list()` lists the loop by that id, though it has no background flag), or letting `decision_close` settle a task-list item when the call comes from a subagent.

response.body:
Two session-decisions changes.

**decision_close from a background subagent ([#37](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/37)).** Inside a subagent, `$.tool.list()` answers the main loop's tools (I confirmed it again on 2.1.300: a background subagent's call listed TaskCreate through TaskUpdate), and no hook lists a subagent's own. So a background subagent was told to use a TaskUpdate it doesn't have, and the ruling went nowhere. The plugin now judges the loop that made the call by its `agentId`:

- the main loop: `$.tool.list()`, as before;
- a subagent spawned in the foreground: what the main loop has (recorded from `agent.spawn`'s `background`);
- a subagent that has called a task tool: it has them;
- any other subagent (background, a teammate, a workflow agent, one spawned before the plugin loaded): no TaskUpdate, so `decision_close` settles the task-list item in the queue, the same path a restart that drops the task tools already takes. `decision_update` points it at that path.

The README's "Without them" paragraph now covers background subagents (their items go through `decision_add` into the shared queue and never reach ctrl+t), and the Limits section says how a subagent is judged.

**Hand-off check ([#1](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/1)).** A `classic.Stop` hook reads the final reply for work handed to the user that isn't queued: list items under a hand-off heading (`Left for you:`, `Next steps for you:`, `You'll need to:`) and lines that hand a step over themselves (`you'll need to merge`, `left for you`, `your call`, `please merge #12`, `run these on each host`). When it finds any, it shows a toast (`2 hand-offs not queued: Merge PR #41.`) and hands the model a reminder with the next prompt through `UserPromptSubmit`'s `additionalContext`. It never blocks, and costs no extra model call. I went with a warning and a nudge rather than the issue's `block`, per its own open question about tuning before blocking.

To keep false alarms rare it skips a line that names a label or that an open item (or one queued this turn) covers by reference or by most of its words; conditional, negated and questioning phrasing; code blocks and quotes; a heading that is really a sentence; and a bare `Next steps:`. It stays quiet while a Stop hook continuation is active, and a new `handoff_check` option turns it off. The detector is `hooks/handoff.ts`, with tests for labelled hand-offs, unlabelled ones, and prose that only resembles one. SKILL.md gets the line that merges and per-host steps count.

Verified on screen with term-recorder (Claude Code 2.1.300, haiku): a reply ending in a `Left for you:` list raised the toast, and on the next prompt ("ok") the model queued both items as A1 and A2. A headless `claude -p` run with a background subagent settled the main loop's A1 through `decision_close`.

Closes #37
Closes #1

response.body:
`/next` ranks issues only. Open PRs never appear, so the thing most likely to be *actually in flight* is invisible in the report that exists to say what to work on.

Observed on `eltorocorp/terraform-et-github` at plugin version `2026.10.15.3`:

```
$ forge-tracker next
Agent-ready ... 15 items, all issues
Blocked         nothing blocked
Flags           8 branches with no PR
```

Meanwhile:

```
$ gh pr list --state open
#260  feat(repos): add mcp-mailgun repository
#259  add helm-forgejo for PoC
#258  Feat/add elboto repo
#254  fix(rulesets): require the dedicated entry point, not et-gh-workflows' own CI
```

None of the four appears anywhere in the report. Confirmed in the facts too, not just the rendering — `forge-tracker next facts --json` gives `in_flight: []` on every one of the 15 items, and `other_branches` lists only branches *without* a PR. There is no PR data in the payload at all.

## This is a spec/implementation gap, not a new feature

#24 already specifies it. From that issue, describing the facts layer:

> **What it reads:** open issues with tier, due date, labels, owners and links; **open PRs/MRs with head pipeline and conflict state**; branches with no PR/MR.

And the `/next` skill text relies on it existing, telling the presenter to keep "each item's in-flight marks (an open PR with its draft, conflict and CI state, or a pushed branch)" and never to call "a lane with `conflicts: unknown` ready to merge". Both instructions are unreachable today, because nothing ever populates `in_flight`.

## Why it bites

The gap is worst in exactly the case the report should be best at. A PR that is open, approved, and stale by a few commits is both the closest thing to done and the easiest to forget; `/next` currently cannot mention it. In the run above, #254 had been open for some weeks, had an approving review, and needed a rebase — none of which surfaced.

It also undercuts lane assignment. A lane cannot be judged safe to start if the report does not know an open PR is already editing those files.

## Shape of the fix

Populate `in_flight` on each item from the PRs that reference it (branch name, `Closes #n`, or a linked issue), and list PRs that reference no issue as their own entries rather than dropping them. The flags section already handles the branch-with-no-PR case; the mirror case, a PR with no issue, has no home today.

Worth carrying through to the report: draft state, mergeable/conflict state (as `unknown` when the forge has not computed it — the skill already says never to present that as clean), review decision, and CI conclusion.

session-decisions picks a repo's forge from its `origin` remote. It uses the built-in host rules and then the `forge_hosts` plugin option from [#57](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/57). Both are global: one host maps to one forge kind for every repo. Some repos need their own answer:

- The remote is an SSH host alias (`github.com-work`, `homelab-git`). The link then uses the alias as its web host, and that host doesn't resolve.
- The remote is a mirror or a push-only URL, and issues live on a different forge. For example, the code is on GitHub but the tracker is a Forgejo instance.
- The SSH host and the web host differ, such as `ssh.git.lab.example.com` against `git.lab.example.com`, or the web UI sits under a subpath.

The fix is a per-repo override that wins over `forge_hosts` and the built-in rules. It would set the forge kind and the web base URL, for example `forgejo` and `https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo`, with an optional host override. Where it could live:

- `git config` in the repo: `git config session-decisions.forge forgejo`, `git config session-decisions.web https://...`. It's per clone, needs no new file, and is read by the same `git` call that already reads the remote.
- The repo's `.claude/settings.json` or `settings.local.json`, under `pluginConfigs`, if Claude Code honours plugin options at project scope.
- A small file in `.claude/`, if forge-tracker ends up with per-repo forge config too, so the two can share it.

forge-tracker resolves the same question for its own reports, so whichever mechanism is chosen should be one both plugins read.

Related: [#54](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/54), [#57](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/57).

Closes [#54](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/54).

## Missing transcript cards

Terminal size wasn't the cause. On Claude Code 2.1.286 a TaskCreate call is folded into a `ToolGroup` with the calls around it (here the ToolSearch that loaded it), and a folded group of those draws nothing on the main view, so the `ToolUse` hook that draws the card never got a row to draw in; ctrl+o unfolds the run, which is why the card showed there. An unfolded group is `ToolUse` rows, which already draw them.

## Clickable references

At session start the plugin reads the `origin` remote (or the only remote) with `git remote get-url`. On github.com, gitlab.com, codeberg.org, or a host named `gitlab.*`, `forgejo.*` or `gitea.*`, it turns `#N`, `!N` and `owner/repo#N` into URLs for that forge:

- the short link on the button row is a `Link` with the reference as its label
- references in the question and qualifier become markdown links
- the More dialog gets a `Link: <url>` line and **Copy link**

On any other host the references stay text, since a self-hosted forge's kind can't be told from its name.

I checked it on screen with term-record, using a scratch repo whose remote is `git@github.com:lokkju/skills.git`. The cast has OSC 8 spans for `!4` (`/pull/4`), `#9` (`/issues/9`) and `#12` (`/issues/12`). The dialog draws its question as plain text, and the cast shows the `Link:` line with no OSC 8 around it. Part of #24.

This adds `/next` for GitHub: the facts, the fingerprint cache, the classification, the unblock counts and the slate (phase 3 of `docs/specs/forge-tracker.md`). By the owner's ruling it comes before phase 2, so it depends on nothing phase 2 builds.

## What /next reports

`forge-tracker next` prints four parts. **Your queue** lists the person-only items, most agent-ready items unblocked first, each with why it's person-only and what it unblocks. **Agent lanes** groups the agent-ready items into lanes Claude judged shouldn't share files, each item marked in flight when it has an open PR (with its draft, conflict and CI state) or a pushed branch. **Blocked** lists each blocked item and what it waits on. **Flags** lists merged-but-open issues, links to closed blockers, blocked labels with nothing linked, blocking cycles, and pushed branches with no PR that name no issue. Until a slate is saved for the current facts, the agent-ready items are listed by tier, agent label, due date and number, and the report ends with `slate: needed`. `commands/next.md` then has Claude read `next facts --json` (which adds issue bodies), build the slate, save it with `next save-slate`, and rerun.

## How it classifies

Person-only means the needs-human or decision label (firm), or a `person_only_markers` word in the title or a label (a hint Claude may overrule in the slate with a reason). Blocked means an open blocker by native link, or the blocked label. Agent-ready means open, not person-only and not blocked (D19): the agent label only sorts items first within their tier. An assignee is never a reason for anything and shows as owner. Unblock counts walk open links with a visited set, so a cycle counts each item once; cycles are found with an iterative Tarjan pass and flagged. Merged-but-open uses real closing references only (`closedByPullRequestsReferences`), never `#N` in a title or branch.

The facts are cached in `next/<host>_<project>/facts.json` with a fingerprint of the cheap reads the spec lists, plus a hash of the config file. While it holds, a rerun makes four requests. A run with a failed read is written but never reused, and no slate is shown or saved over it. Every read fails on its own and none renders as empty: if the blocking links fail, items that would be agent-ready show as not classified; if the issues read fails, every section says FAILED.

## The phase-2 seam

Phase 2's pickup record (branch to issue) doesn't exist yet. `next.recorded_pickups` is the single place that would read it; it returns none for now, and `classify` already accepts pickups with `via: "pickup"` (a test covers that path). Until then, an issue is in flight only through what the forge shows: an open PR with a closing reference to it, `#N` in an open PR's title, or `N` as a segment of a PR's or pushed branch's name.

## Reads

The adapter gains two reads: `fingerprint_inputs` (one GraphQL query for the default-branch head, open counts and newest update times, plus paginated milestones and branch heads, plus `actions/runs?per_page=1`) and `closing_refs` (GraphQL over open issues; more closing references than one page holds is a FAILED read, not a short list). `Issue` now carries its body. All requests are GETs or GraphQL queries through the existing guard.

## Tests

`tests/test_next.py` builds a fake forge with a decision that unblocks a chain, a needs-human item, a marker hint, tiers and the agent label, an in-flight PR and branch, a merged-but-open issue, a blocked label with nothing linked, a stale link and a cycle. It checks the text report against a golden, the JSON classification, the 0600 cache and fingerprint reuse, `--refresh`, a config change moving the fingerprint, failed reads (never reused, never shown as empty, tokens redacted), the saved slate with its age, `--rerank`, a moved fingerprint, every `save-slate` refusal, and that `save-slate` touches no forge. There are unit tests for transitive and cycle-safe unblock counts, a 1500-item chain, marker word matching, cross-project blockers, pickups and branch-number parsing. A `/next` run recorded from this repo replays against a golden report, and the adapter's new reads join the contract suite. 196 tests pass on Python 3.9 and 3.14.

## Open questions

1. **A blocked label with nothing linked counts as blocked.** The spec's `/groom` treats it as drift and proposes removing the label; `/next` still treats it as blocked and flags it, since calling it agent-ready would trust the label less than the person who set it.
2. **The config file is part of the fingerprint.** The spec's list doesn't include it, but classification and the slate depend on its labels, tiers and markers, so a config change asks for a new slate.
3. **A blocked person-only item goes under Blocked, not Your queue.**
4. **Unblock counts walk through person-only items but don't count them.** If P blocks Q (person-only) and Q blocks A, P's count includes A.
5. **The newest pipeline time moves while CI runs.** That's in the spec's fingerprint, but it means a slate saved during a CI run goes stale when the run finishes. A per-commit check state (or excluding in-progress runs) would be steadier.
6. **Sub-issues aren't read.** The spec's table lists GraphQL `subIssues` next to `blockedBy`, but nothing says parent and child are a blocking relation, so only `blockedBy` counts.

Adds **term-recorder**, which lets an assistant see a terminal program the way a person does. `term-record` runs a command on a private tmux server, drives it from a step file of keystrokes, waits and clicks, and captures the result as plain-text screen snaps, an asciicast and a GIF through agg. It came out of checking how session-decisions' More dialog renders, which reading the source couldn't answer.

**Isolation.** The command runs on its own server (`tmux -L term-record-<pid>`) with a generated config and no status line, so it never touches your tmux server or `~/.tmux.conf`. It starts with a minimal environment (HOME, PATH, USER, LOGNAME, SHELL, LANG, LC_ALL, LC_CTYPE, TMPDIR), plus whatever `--env` and `--pass` add, and the server is killed when the run ends. The default size is 100x30.

**Steps.** A step file supports `wait`, `gone`, `idle`, `keys`, `type`, `paste`, `click`, `sleep`, `snap`, `record`, `include` and `when`, with shell quoting and `--var` substitution. A failed step exits 1, names the file and line, and prints the screen. `examples/claude-start.steps` gets a fresh Claude Code session past folder trust, and `examples/ask-dialog.steps` snaps its question dialog with a multi-line markdown question.

**Permissions.** The skill's `allowed-tools` is `Bash(${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/term-record *)`, so installing the plugin is the grant, scoped to the turn the skill is used in. Nobody edits settings.

**Ported from record-demo.sh.** Setting `window-size manual` in a startup config crashes tmux 3.4's server, so it's set after the session exists, as record-demo.sh already did.

**Not in this PR.** Converting `record-demo.sh` to a term-recorder step file is a follow-up.

**Checks.** The 20 tests pass locally, driving real tmux sessions against shell and Python targets. `claude plugin validate --strict` passes for the marketplace and the plugin, and so does `check-skill-names.py`. CI installs tmux for this plugin's matrix entry.

Stacked on [lokkju/skills#38](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/38) (the design). The base is `main`, so until #38 merges this PR's diff also shows #38's commits; merge #38 first.

Phase 1 of `docs/specs/forge-tracker.md`, for [lokkju/skills#21](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/21) and [lokkju/skills#23](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/23) on GitHub: the plugin skeleton, the read-only GitHub layer and `/catchup`.

- **Transport** (`scripts/forge_tracker/transport.py`): every request passes `check_read` before it's sent. GET is allowed; a POST is allowed only to the GraphQL endpoint and only when every operation in the document is a query, found by tokenizing the document (strings, block strings and comments skipped), so a mutation after a query, a subscription, or a document that doesn't parse is refused before the network is touched. Lists follow `Link` (or `X-Next-Page`) to the last page, and a page cap that is hit fails the read with the cap named. Error text is cut to 300 characters with token shapes and the token in use replaced by `***`.
- **Detection and config**: `forge:` from `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md`, else the origin host (github.com; GitLab and unknown hosts stop with a message). The glab host check and the `/api/v1/version` probe come with the GitLab and Forgejo phases. The config loader reads the frontmatter's strict YAML subset with the standard library and fails on any unknown key.
- **GitHub adapter**: `urllib` with the token from `gh auth token` (the spec's transport table now says so, last commit). REST for issues, comments, search mentions, Actions runs and jobs, tags, releases and branches; GraphQL for open PRs (`mergeable`, review requests, head status), merged PRs (`closingIssuesReferences`) and native `blockedBy` links. Mergeability is yes, no or unknown.
- **`/catchup`** (`commands/catchup.md`, `forge-tracker catchup`): the five sections in the spec's order, text or `--json`, exit 1 when any read failed. The marker is `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/forge-tracker/catchup/<host>_<project>_<user>.json`, 0600 in 0700 directories; the new one is written to a temp file, the report prints, then it's renamed into place, and a failed print or a failed read leaves the old one. `--since` and `--no-mark` don't move it; the window opens five minutes before it.
- `forge-tracker smoke` runs every read once and prints counts, for #21's live run.
- Wiring: marketplace entry, README catalog, AGENTS.md layout, the `forge-tracker` yeet target (`forge-tracker--v`, `plugin.json` version `0.0.0` until yeet's first release writes it), and CI's forge-release job turned into a matrix over both Python plugins.

**Tests**: 143 pytest tests, no network, passing on Python 3.9, 3.11 and 3.14. `tests/fixtures/github/catchup-lokkju-skills.json` is a real `catchup --since 1d` against this repo, recorded with `--record` (tokens scrubbed, REST bulk fields no adapter reads dropped) and replayed against a golden report. The edge cases a live repo rarely has at once (unknown and conflicting mergeability, retried jobs, bots, page caps, each read failing alone, the marker rules) are built in the tests. `claude plugin validate --strict` passes on the marketplace and all three plugins.

**Live run**: `forge-tracker smoke` against lokkju/skills read everything (11 open issues, 2 open PRs with mergeability known, 17 merged in 7 days, 0 blocking links), and `catchup --since 5d` printed a full report in about 2 seconds.

_Moved from my private repo, where it was skills-marketplace#6._

The forge-release skill's decision tree currently routes CalVer (and anything on GitLab or Azure DevOps) to yeet, SemVer packages on GitHub to release-please, and Rust crates to release-plz. The question is whether the middle branch should go to yeet too, so one tool covers every non-crate repo. The python-project skill's release-please default would follow whatever this decides.

## The case for keeping release-please, checked

- **Native version files.** Weaker than it sounds. Neither tool updates `uv.lock`: release-please has googleapis/release-please#2561 open for it. yeet updates `pyproject.toml` through a marker comment (`version = "1.2.3" # x-yeet-version`) and `package.json` through `json_pointer: /version`, which covers the files these repos publish from.
- **Tokens.** No difference. Both run on `GITHUB_TOKEN` when the publish step lives in the release workflow, and both need a GitHub App token only when the release has to start another workflow (one of my sites' deploy does).
- **Maturity.** The real one. yeet (monkescience/yeet, MIT) was created in February 2026 and has 4 contributors and 7 stars; release-please is Google's and widely used.
- **Language plugins.** release-please has strategies and plugins for Java, Ruby, PHP, Helm and node or cargo workspaces. None of these repos use them.

## Why the maturity risk is small here

- yeet runs as a container pinned by digest, so an abandoned yeet keeps working at the pinned version.
- Its only state is git tags and `CHANGELOG.md`, both tool-agnostic, so leaving it is a config swap. yeet's docs carry a migrate-from-release-please guide, and the reverse is the same shape.
- Telemetry is on by default; the skill already sets `telemetry.enabled: false` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.

## What standardizing gets

One tool, one `.yeet.yaml` shape and one App pattern across GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps, for CalVer and SemVer. The skill's decision tree drops a branch, and its references drop the release-please setup and troubleshooting.

## Proposal

- New repos: yeet, SemVer or CalVer.
- Rust crates: release-plz stays. It publishes to crates.io and runs cargo-semver-checks, which yeet doesn't.
- Repos on release-please today move only when someone is in them anyway: lokkju/dbxdebug, lokkju/git-spreader and two private repos. release-plz today: lokkju/neovision and two private repos.
- python-project switches its release default to yeet.

## Not yet checked

- How yeet handles a Python package whose `uv.lock` records the project's own version (a release PR that bumps `pyproject.toml` but not `uv.lock` would fail `uv sync --locked`). release-please has the same gap; the usual fixes are a dynamic version (hatch-vcs) or a follow-up `uv lock` commit on the release branch.
- yeet's monorepo targets against release-please's linked versions, if a multi-package repo ever needs them.

`decision_close` now settles a task-list item only when TaskUpdate isn't in the session's tool list. Fixes #26.

The facts behind this are in [the issue comment](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/26#issuecomment-6180088351). In short: `--resume`, `--continue` and compaction keep the session id; backgrounding a session forks it under a new id and copies its task files into `tasks/<new id>` (unless `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` is set, when nothing is copied and the list is shared). That is what happened in #9: `session:b54339de-…` in the store still holds A38 to A40, and the backgrounded job `3eb3b414` read its own, empty record.

**Changes, in `hooks/register.tsx`:**
- **Forks.** A session with no record whose task files hold decision items adopts the record of the stored session whose task list holds every one of those items by task id and label, with at least one word for word; the most recently used one wins. The fork gets a copy, and the parent keeps its own.
- **Shared task lists.** With `CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID` set, the record is `list:<id>`. A `session:<sid>` record for the same session moves under it on the first read. `persist` merges with what's stored, keeping the higher counters, every creation time and every ledger item (the settled copy wins), so two sessions on one list don't erase each other's ledger.
- **`prune`** keeps the 100 most recently used records across both key kinds.
- **`--continue`.** `$.session.id()` read in `classic.SessionStart` returns a placeholder id under `--continue`, while the hook input's `session_id` is right. The resume hook now hydrates with `e.session_id`.

**Tests:** seven new cases in `tests/register.test.tsx`: the list-keyed record and concurrent writes to it, a new session id on the same list keeping counters, ledger and rulings, migration of an old session record, a fork adopting its parent's record (and not a stranger whose list has the same ids and labels), a fresh session adopting nothing, the resume hook using the input's id, and prune across both key kinds. Six of them fail against `main`. The test engine now keeps several task lists and its own in-memory store, so a test can seed what an earlier process left. `claude plugin test`: 53 pass. `claude plugin validate --strict` and `tsc` pass.

**Not verified:** a real background fork against this plugin (it can't be triggered headless; the behaviour comes from the engine's code and the #9 files), and a daemon restart of a job, which on the evidence of the job directories keeps its session id.

The TaskCreate hook rejected this subject with "a DECIDE item needs a recommendation, written as (recommend <choice>)":

```
DECIDE: what to work on next in lokkju/skills? (recommend: ship release #16 now, then a session-decisions hardening release (#14 rest, #4 skill wording, #20, triage #15 and #13), then settle #10 and write the forge-release skill #11, then forge-tracker) [https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues]
```

At the time it looked like the nested parenthetical was the cause. It isn't: `CHOICE` in `hooks/subject.ts` already allows one nested level, and this body without the colon passes `problems()` and yields the full choice from `recommendation()`. The cause is the colon in `(recommend: ...`. `RECOMMEND` is `/\(recommend\s+\S/i`, so `(recommend:` never matches, and the error message doesn't say so.

Two things to fix:

- Accept `(recommend: <choice>)` as well as `(recommend <choice>)` in `problems()`, `recommendation()` and `splitBody()`. Models write the colon form naturally.
- `recommendation()` and `splitBody()` handle one level of nesting only. A choice with two nested levels passes validation but loses its Accept button and its recommends tag. Matching the closing parenthesis by depth instead of by regex removes the limit.

The rejected subject in #27 was written as `(recommend: ...)`. The hook's check required whitespace right after `recommend`, so the colon form failed; the nested parenthetical was already handled. This change:

## What happens

After a session resumes (here: the user ran `/exit` and the background job restarted), the harness no longer offers `TaskCreate`, `TaskGet`, `TaskList` or `TaskUpdate`, but the session-decisions queue still lists the task-list items created before the restart. Those items can't be settled any more:

- `TaskUpdate` isn't available, so the documented way to close a task-list item is gone.
- `decision_close` refuses them: `session-decisions: A37 isn't in the fallback ledger. If it's a task-list item, mark it completed with TaskUpdate and add the ruling to its description.`

So a finished item (A37 here) keeps showing in the SessionStart reminder ("Open items in this session's decision queue, still waiting on the user") and in the UI, and the user reasonably asks why it's still open.

New items in the same session correctly fall back to `decision_add` (they get ledger labels, e.g. A38, A39), so the labels keep counting; only closing pre-restart task-list items is stuck.

## Repro

1. In a background session with task tools, create an ACTION item via TaskCreate (gets A37).
2. Restart the session so the task tools are no longer offered (resume after `/exit` in a background job).
3. Try to close it: `decision_close` with label A37 is refused; no TaskUpdate exists.

## Suggested fix

Either:
- let `decision_close` settle a task-list item when the task tools aren't available (record the ruling in the plugin's own store and mark the item closed there, so the reminder and UI stop listing it; reconcile if TaskUpdate comes back), or
- have the SessionStart reminder and UI read the task list's real status and drop items the harness can no longer update, with a note.

The first keeps "every hand-off is a queue item" working across restarts. A test: create via the tasks source, simulate no task tools, close via `decision_close`, expect the item closed and absent from the reminder.

Related: [lokkju/skills#7](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/7) (TaskUpdate subject edits dropping labels).

## What happens

When a decision item's subject is changed with `TaskUpdate` and the new subject is written the way the skill tells the assistant to write subjects (`DECIDE: ... (recommend X) [link]`, no label), the task ends up with no `D<N>`/`A<N>` label. The task list then shows items like `DECIDE: approve the agent dispatcher spec ...` with no number, and the queue can't refer to them.

Seen in an infra session on 2026-10-10/11: five items (D65, A24, D71, D72, D73) lost their labels after their questions were revised per the "revise open decisions" practice.

## Why

`hooks/register.tsx`, the `TaskUpdate` handler, runs `next(e)` with `e.subject` unchanged and only then mirrors the change with `applyUpdate`. The `TaskCreate` handler rewrites the subject to add the label before the tool runs; the `TaskUpdate` handler has no equivalent, so the stored task subject is the unlabelled draft. In `hooks/queue.ts`, `applyUpdate` then reparses the new subject with `itemFromTask`, which (for an unlabelled draft) either drops the item or rebuilds it without its label.

## Suggested fix

In the `TaskUpdate` handler, before `next(e)`: if `e.subject` parses as a draft (`parseDraft`) and the task is an existing item, rewrite `e.subject` to `formatSubject(current.label, draft)`, keeping the item's label (and refuse a kind change, or allow it with a new label). Also run `problems(draft)` so a revised DECIDE still needs a recommendation and a link. A test in `tests/queue.test.ts` for "update with an unlabelled draft keeps the label".

The SKILL.md could also say that a revised subject keeps its label, though the hook fixing it is better than relying on the assistant.

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21), plus a small set of writes.

**`/groom`** keeps the tracker telling the truth, so that `/catchup` and `/next` rank real work. In practice the board drifts in predictable ways, and a ranking built on a drifted board ranks finished work as ready.

**The checks:**
- **Merged but still open:** an issue that a merged PR/MR references (`Closes #N`, `#N` in the title or branch) but that is still open. This is verified against the default branch, not taken on trust.
- **Labels disagreeing with milestones:** a tier label with no matching milestone, or a milestone whose tier label is missing.
- **A blocked label with nothing linked**, or links whose blocker is closed.
- **Decided but still waiting:** an issue labelled needs-a-human or decision that has a ruling comment after the label was added.
- **Stale branches:** remote branches with no open PR/MR whose commits are all on the default branch, so they are candidates to delete.
- **Stale or conflicted PRs/MRs:** open ones with merge conflicts, or no activity for N days.
- **Likely duplicates:** title and term similarity among open issues and those closed recently.
- **Placeholder due dates** shared by many issues, which skew any ordering by due date.

**Behaviour:**
- **Report first, read-only by default.** Every proposed change is listed with its evidence. Nothing is written until the user approves, item by item or as a batch.
- **Approved writes:** close with a resolution comment naming the PR/MR, fix labels or milestones, remove a blocked label, delete a merged branch. Each goes through forge-tracker's optional write-wrapper (#12), so a repo can enforce its own scrubbing or comment format.
- **Never acts on an inference it couldn't verify:** an "unclear" bucket is left for the user.
- **Output:** text and `--json`, with FAILED reads stated plainly, never as an empty section.

`github-app-create` could only make a private App and store installation credentials. The homelab's github-mcp-server wants a read-only App, installed on my account and my organizations, whose user access token (`ghu_...`) acts as me ([lokkju/infra#172](https://github.com/lokkju/infra/pull/172)). A private App can't be installed outside its owner's account, and nothing obtained a user token.

- `--public` sets the manifest's `public: true`. After the first install the script prints `https://github.com/apps/<slug>/installations/new` for each further account. The README says what public means and that anything using installation tokens should check each installation's owner.
- `--user-token` (needs `--to sops`) puts the local listener's `/callback` in the manifest's `callback_urls`, and after the install runs the web authorization flow with `state` and PKCE. It then trades the code at `login/oauth/access_token` using the `client_secret` from the manifest conversion and encrypts the token under `--sops-key` (default `token`). The private key isn't stored in this mode.
- Expiry: the manifest has no field for it, so a new App's user tokens expire after 8 hours, with a 6-month refresh token. `--opt-out-expiry` pauses before the authorization so you can opt out in the App's settings, which gets a token that doesn't expire. Without the flag, `refresh_token`, `client_id` and `client_secret` go into the same Secret for a refresh job.
- No `--no-webhook`: the manifest already has no `hook_attributes` (GitHub rejects the block without a url), so the App never has a webhook. The README now says so.
- `store.sops_store_values` writes several keys in one pass, with the same copy, rename and read-back checks. `sops_store_key` wraps it.

- **Structure:** one `SKILL.md` with the decision tree and flow, `references/` per topic (yeet, release-please, release-plz, deploy workflow, migration, troubleshooting), and `templates/` made generic from a working migration's files (`yeet.yml`, `.yeet.yaml`, the deploy guards). - **Decision tree:** yeet for CalVer and for anything on GitLab or Azure DevOps, release-please for SemVer packages on GitHub, release-plz for Rust crates, pending #10 (standardize on yeet).

## Lessons to carry in

- yeet's `--dry-run` needs local HEAD to equal the release branch's remote head; a scratch `--config` copy with `branch:` changed works around it.
- A bare first-of-day tag (`vYYYY.MM.DD`) is invisible to yeet; retag it `.1`.
- yeet needs a GitHub App token for its release to start other workflows; `github-app-create` must not send `hook_attributes` without a URL, and adding repos to an installation needs a classic token (a gh OAuth token gets 403), so repo access is set in the App's settings.
- Telemetry is on by default: `telemetry.enabled: false` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.

session-decisions now reads a per-clone forge override from git config ([#70](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/70), for [#60](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/60)):

```
git config tracker.forge forgejo
git config tracker.web https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo
```

The keys are named `tracker.*` so that forge-tracker can read them too. forge-tracker still works out the forge only from `origin` and its own `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` (`forge:`). A repo whose remote is an SSH alias, a mirror or a push-only URL therefore gets correct links from session-decisions and still fails or misreads in `/catchup` and `/next`.

forge-tracker should read `tracker.forge` and `tracker.web` with `git config --get`, with the same precedence session-decisions uses:
- `tracker.web` replaces the remote's host and path;
- `tracker.forge` sets the kind;
- both win over the built-in host rules.

Its existing `forge:` key in `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` should either defer to `tracker.forge` or be documented as the committed per-repo default, with git config as the per-clone override. The API base for a self-hosted forge (and any pinned CA) still comes from forge-tracker's own config, since git config holds only the web base.

response.body:
A clone can now say which forge its `#12` and `!4` references link to, ahead of `forge_hosts` and the built-in host rules:

```bash
git config tracker.forge forgejo
git config tracker.web https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo
```

## Why git config

I weighed the three places [#60](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/60) names:

- **git config** is per clone, which is where an SSH host alias belongs (it comes from one machine's `~/.ssh/config`, so a committed file would be wrong for other clones). git parses it, the plugin reads it with one more `git` call next to the remote lookup, and forge-tracker's Python can read it with `git config --get` and no parser. `includeIf "hasconfig:remote.*.url:..."` in `~/.gitconfig` can apply `tracker.forge` to every clone of an alias.
- **Project-scoped plugin options** are per plugin, so forge-tracker couldn't read session-decisions' value without reaching into another plugin's settings, and `.claude/settings.json` is committed.
- **A `.claude/` file**: forge-tracker already has `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` with a `forge:` key, but its loader rejects unknown keys (there's no `web:`), session-decisions would need a frontmatter parser, and a committed file has the same alias problem.

The keys are `tracker.*`, not `session-decisions.*`, so both plugins can read them. Magit Forge already uses the `forge.*` section, so I avoided that one.

## Behaviour

- `tracker.web` set: it is the repository (`https://` only), and the remote isn't read. The kind is `tracker.forge`, or else whatever `forge_hosts` and the built-in rules say of the web host.
- Only `tracker.forge` set: the remote's host and path on that kind of forge.
- Neither set: the existing behaviour, unchanged.
- A subpath works for GitHub and Forgejo (`https://code.example.org/forge/me/tool`, cross-repo refs included). For GitLab the whole path is the project, so `group/project#7` misses a subpath; the README says so.
- A value it can't use gets a toast at session start, the same way `forge_hosts` does, and is ignored.

The pure logic (`parseOverride`, `webForge`, `resolveForge`) lives in `hooks/forge.ts` with tests; `register.tsx` reads `git config --get-regexp '^tracker\.(forge|web)$'` at session start.

## Verified

- `claude plugin test plugins/session-decisions`: 93 pass. `claude plugin validate --strict plugins/session-decisions` passes.
- On screen with term-recorder: Claude Code 2.1.300, Sonnet, `--plugin-dir` on this branch, in a scratch repo whose `origin` is `homelab-git:lokkju/demo.git` with both keys set. One `DECIDE ... [#12]` task drew the D1 card, and the cast has the OSC 8 hyperlink `https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo/issues/12` on its `#12`.
- The `includeIf hasconfig` glob in the README (`homelab-git:*/**`) was checked against git 2.43; `homelab-git:**` doesn't match a path with a slash.

forge-tracker doesn't read the keys yet; that's a follow-up there.

Closes #60

session-decisions picks a repo's forge from its `origin` remote. It uses the built-in host rules and then the `forge_hosts` plugin option from [#57](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/57). Both are global: one host maps to one forge kind for every repo. Some repos need their own answer:

- The remote is an SSH host alias (`github.com-work`, `homelab-git`). The link then uses the alias as its web host, and that host doesn't resolve.
- The remote is a mirror or a push-only URL, and issues live on a different forge. For example, the code is on GitHub but the tracker is a Forgejo instance.
- The SSH host and the web host differ, such as `ssh.git.lab.example.com` against `git.lab.example.com`, or the web UI sits under a subpath.

The fix is a per-repo override that wins over `forge_hosts` and the built-in rules. It would set the forge kind and the web base URL, for example `forgejo` and `https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo`, with an optional host override. Where it could live:

- `git config` in the repo: `git config session-decisions.forge forgejo`, `git config session-decisions.web https://...`. It's per clone, needs no new file, and is read by the same `git` call that already reads the remote.
- The repo's `.claude/settings.json` or `settings.local.json`, under `pluginConfigs`, if Claude Code honours plugin options at project scope.
- A small file in `.claude/`, if forge-tracker ends up with per-repo forge config too, so the two can share it.

forge-tracker resolves the same question for its own reports, so whichever mechanism is chosen should be one both plugins read.

Related: [#54](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/54), [#57](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/57).

Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21), plus a small set of writes.

**`/groom`** keeps the tracker telling the truth, so that `/catchup` and `/next` rank real work. In practice the board drifts in predictable ways, and a ranking built on a drifted board ranks finished work as ready.

**The checks:**
- **Merged but still open:** an issue that a merged PR/MR references (`Closes #N`, `#N` in the title or branch) but that is still open. This is verified against the default branch, not taken on trust.
- **Labels disagreeing with milestones:** a tier label with no matching milestone, or a milestone whose tier label is missing.
- **A blocked label with nothing linked**, or links whose blocker is closed.
- **Decided but still waiting:** an issue labelled needs-a-human or decision that has a ruling comment after the label was added.
- **Stale branches:** remote branches with no open PR/MR whose commits are all on the default branch, so they are candidates to delete.
- **Stale or conflicted PRs/MRs:** open ones with merge conflicts, or no activity for N days.
- **Likely duplicates:** title and term similarity among open issues and those closed recently.
- **Placeholder due dates** shared by many issues, which skew any ordering by due date.

**Behaviour:**
- **Report first, read-only by default.** Every proposed change is listed with its evidence. Nothing is written until the user approves, item by item or as a batch.
- **Approved writes:** close with a resolution comment naming the PR/MR, fix labels or milestones, remove a blocked label, delete a merged branch. Each goes through forge-tracker's optional write-wrapper (#12), so a repo can enforce its own scrubbing or comment format.
- **Never acts on an inference it couldn't verify:** an "unclear" bucket is left for the user.
- **Output:** text and `--json`, with FAILED reads stated plainly, never as an empty section.

response.body:
Part of #12 (forge-tracker). A read-only forge layer that the briefing and grooming commands use. It is filed as its own piece, because the three commands built on it each need the same reads on all three forges.

**The forges.** GitHub (`gh`, REST plus GraphQL where REST is thin), GitLab (`glab api`, including self-hosted with a subpath and a pinned CA) and Forgejo/Gitea (`tea` where it covers the read, otherwise the REST API with the user's token). Each forge is detected from the repo's remote, the same way #12 already plans.

**What every adapter answers, in one normalized shape:**
- **Identity:** the authenticated user, and whether an account is a bot.
- **Issues:** open issues, and issues updated since a time. Each carries labels, milestone (title, due date), assignees, created/updated/closed timestamps and comments since a time.
- **Links between issues:** native blocking where the forge has it (GitHub "blocked by" issue dependencies and sub-issues, Forgejo dependencies, GitLab `blocks` on tiers that have it). Where it doesn't (GitLab CE has only `relates_to`), a configurable convention such as `relates_to` plus a `blocked` label.
- **PRs/MRs:** open, and merged since a time. Each carries title, source branch, merge commit sha, reviewers/assignees, draft and conflict state, and head pipeline status.
- **CI:** the newest pipeline/workflow run on the default branch by trigger (push vs schedule), its failed jobs, and jobs that passed only on retry.
- **Branches:** remote branch heads, and which have no open PR/MR.
- **Tags/releases:** the newest tags and releases. Container registry tags are optional, and only where configured.

**Rules learned building this once:**
- **GET only, enforced at the boundary.** The adapter's transport refuses any method but GET, so a read-only command can't write even by mistake.
- **Paginate to the end, or fail loudly.** A page cap that is hit is a FAILED read, never a silently short list that renders as "none".
- **Every read can fail on its own.** It returns data or a named error, and callers print `<part>: FAILED (<reason>)`, never an empty section.
- **The shared account.** Agents usually authenticate as the user, so nothing may treat "the user's account did X" as "the user did X", and no assignee is a signal that a human must act.
- **No secrets in errors.** Error text includes the CLI's stderr truncated, never tokens.
- **Injectable fetch.** Tests feed canned payloads per forge, with no network.

**Done when:** each forge's adapter passes the same contract test suite over recorded fixtures, plus one live read-only smoke run per forge.
response.title: forge-tracker: a read-only forge layer for GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo

- **Structure:** one `SKILL.md` with the decision tree and flow, `references/` per topic (yeet, release-please, release-plz, deploy workflow, migration, troubleshooting), and `templates/` made generic from a working migration's files (`yeet.yml`, `.yeet.yaml`, the deploy guards). - yeet's `--dry-run` needs local HEAD to equal the release branch's remote head; a scratch `--config` copy with `branch:` changed works around it.
- A bare first-of-day tag (`vYYYY.MM.DD`) is invisible to yeet; retag it `.1`.

- Self-hosted runners:
  - Without a Docker daemon, run yeet from its release tarball checked against a pinned SHA-256 instead of `docker://`.
  - Runners that export `GITHUB_URL` (GARM does) make yeet call `/api/v3/...` as if on GitHub Enterprise; set `GITHUB_URL: ""` in the yeet step.
  - Cache paths follow `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, which may not be `~/.cache`.
- Private repos fetching fresh tags in a deploy need `git -c credential.helper='!gh auth git-credential'`.
- Deploy guards: deploy only from main, only the newest release tag, and create nothing (no tags, no releases) in the deploy workflow. Filter "newest tag" to the release shape so a stray `v*` tag can't block deploys.
- A shared deploy concurrency group can cancel a queued run.

response.body:
_Moved from my private repo, where it was skills-marketplace#6._

The forge-release skill's decision tree currently routes CalVer (and anything on GitLab or Azure DevOps) to yeet, SemVer packages on GitHub to release-please, and Rust crates to release-plz. The question is whether the middle branch should go to yeet too, so one tool covers every non-crate repo. The python-project skill's release-please default would follow whatever this decides.

## The case for keeping release-please, checked

- **Native version files.** Weaker than it sounds. Neither tool updates `uv.lock`: release-please has googleapis/release-please#2561 open for it. yeet updates `pyproject.toml` through a marker comment (`version = "1.2.3" # x-yeet-version`) and `package.json` through `json_pointer: /version`, which covers the files these repos publish from.
- **Tokens.** No difference. Both run on `GITHUB_TOKEN` when the publish step lives in the release workflow, and both need a GitHub App token only when the release has to start another workflow (one of my sites' deploy does).
- **Maturity.** The real one. yeet (monkescience/yeet, MIT) was created in February 2026 and has 4 contributors and 7 stars; release-please is Google's and widely used.
- **Language plugins.** release-please has strategies and plugins for Java, Ruby, PHP, Helm and node or cargo workspaces. None of these repos use them.

## Why the maturity risk is small here

- yeet runs as a container pinned by digest, so an abandoned yeet keeps working at the pinned version.
- Its only state is git tags and `CHANGELOG.md`, both tool-agnostic, so leaving it is a config swap. yeet's docs carry a migrate-from-release-please guide, and the reverse is the same shape.
- Telemetry is on by default; the skill already sets `telemetry.enabled: false` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.

## What standardizing gets

One tool, one `.yeet.yaml` shape and one App pattern across GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps, for CalVer and SemVer. The skill's decision tree drops a branch, and its references drop the release-please setup and troubleshooting.

## Proposal

- New repos: yeet, SemVer or CalVer.
- Rust crates: release-plz stays. It publishes to crates.io and runs cargo-semver-checks, which yeet doesn't.
- Repos on release-please today move only when someone is in them anyway: lokkju/dbxdebug, lokkju/git-spreader and two private repos. release-plz today: lokkju/neovision and two private repos.
- python-project switches its release default to yeet.

## Not yet checked

- How yeet handles a Python package whose `uv.lock` records the project's own version (a release PR that bumps `pyproject.toml` but not `uv.lock` would fail `uv sync --locked`). release-please has the same gap; the usual fixes are a dynamic version (hatch-vcs) or a follow-up `uv lock` commit on the release branch.
- yeet's monorepo targets against release-please's linked versions, if a multi-package repo ever needs them.
